items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we are given two vectors
[MATH: \mathbf{a} = \langle 2,3 \rangle] and [MATH: \mathbf{b} = \langle -4,4 \rangle,] shown below. How do we compute the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}] and [MATH: -5\mathbf{a}] in terms of the standard basis [MATH: \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4c41d04b963e9ff1e860fc815a80133d]

Content:
To compute [MATH: \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b},] we collect all of the [MATH: \mathbf{i}]'s and [MATH: \mathbf{j}]'s. We know that [MATH: \mathbf{a} = {\color{red}2}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}3}\mathbf{j}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b} = {\color{red}-4}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}4}\mathbf{j}.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: a + b|= (2i + 3j) + (− 4i + 4j); = (2 + (− 4))i + (3 + 4)j; = − 2i + 7j.]

Content:
Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get
[MATH: [− 2; 7]]

Content:
To compute [MATH: -5\mathbf{a},] we multiply each of the components by [MATH: -5\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: − 5 ⋅ a|= − 5(2i + 3j); = (− 5 ⋅ 2)i + (− 5 ⋅ 3)j; = − 10i + − 15j]

Content:
Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get
[MATH: [− 10; − 15]]

items.readable_text:
Content:
To add or subtract vectors given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to add or subtract each component separately.

Content:
For example, in angle bracket notation, we have
[MATH: ⟨2, 5⟩ + ⟨− 3, 7⟩|=; ⟨2 + (− 3), 5 + 7⟩|=; ⟨− 1, 12⟩|,]

Content:
and in column vector notation, we have
[MATH: [2; 5] + [− 3; 7]|= [2 + (− 3); 5 + 7] = [− 1; 12].]

Content:
Likewise, to multiply a vector given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to multiply each component separately.

Content:
For example, in angle bracket notation, we have
[MATH: − 5 ⋅ ⟨2, 5⟩|=; ⟨(− 5) ⋅ 2, (− 5) ⋅ 5⟩|=; ⟨− 10, − 25⟩|,]

Content:
and in column vector notation, we have
[MATH: − 5 ⋅ [2; 5]|= [(− 5) ⋅ 2; (− 5) ⋅ 5] = [− 10; − 25].]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we are given two vectors
[MATH: \mathbf{a} = \langle 2,3 \rangle] and [MATH: \mathbf{b} = \langle -4,4 \rangle,] shown below. How do we compute the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}] and [MATH: -5\mathbf{a}] in terms of the standard basis [MATH: \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}?]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4c41d04b963e9ff1e860fc815a80133d]

Content:
To compute [MATH: \mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b},] we collect all of the [MATH: \mathbf{i}]'s and [MATH: \mathbf{j}]'s. We know that [MATH: \mathbf{a} = {\color{red}2}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}3}\mathbf{j}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b} = {\color{red}-4}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}4}\mathbf{j}.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: a + b|= (2i + 3j) + (− 4i + 4j); = (2 + (− 4))i + (3 + 4)j; = − 2i + 7j.]

Content:
Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get
[MATH: [− 2; 7]]

Content:
To compute [MATH: -5\mathbf{a},] we multiply each of the components by [MATH: -5\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: − 5 ⋅ a|= − 5(2i + 3j); = (− 5 ⋅ 2)i + (− 5 ⋅ 3)j; = − 10i + − 15j]

Content:
Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get
[MATH: [− 10; − 15]]

---

Item 2 — Example: Addition and Scalar Multiplication of Vectors in Component Form

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: \mathbf{a}-2\mathbf{b}] if [MATH: \mathbf{a}=-4\mathbf{i}+6\mathbf{j}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}=12\mathbf{i}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To compute [MATH: \mathbf{a}-2\mathbf{b},] we just need to compute all of the [MATH: \mathbf{i}]'s and [MATH: \mathbf{j}]'s, as follows:
[MATH: a − 2b|= (− 4i + 6j) − 2(12i); = − 4i + 6j − 24i; = (− 4i − 24i) + 6j; = − 28i + 6j]

---

Item 3 — Question 1

Prompt:
Find [MATH: 2a + b] if [MATH: a = 4i + 2j] and [MATH: b = 6i − 4j.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Sums and Scalar Multiplication of Vectors in Angle Bracket or Column Vector Form

Content:
To add or subtract vectors given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to add or subtract each component separately.

Content:
For example, in angle bracket notation, we have
[MATH: ⟨2, 5⟩ + ⟨− 3, 7⟩|=; ⟨2 + (− 3), 5 + 7⟩|=; ⟨− 1, 12⟩|,]

Content:
and in column vector notation, we have
[MATH: [2; 5] + [− 3; 7]|= [2 + (− 3); 5 + 7] = [− 1; 12].]

Content:
Likewise, to multiply a vector given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to multiply each component separately.

Content:
For example, in angle bracket notation, we have
[MATH: − 5 ⋅ ⟨2, 5⟩|=; ⟨(− 5) ⋅ 2, (− 5) ⋅ 5⟩|=; ⟨− 10, − 25⟩|,]

Content:
and in column vector notation, we have
[MATH: − 5 ⋅ [2; 5]|= [(− 5) ⋅ 2; (− 5) ⋅ 5] = [− 10; − 25].]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Common Notations Used When Describing Vectors

Content:
To denote a vector, we have used two notations:

Content:
- a single bold lowercase letter, such as [MATH: \mathbf{v},] or
- two uppercase letters representing the points of the ends of the vector, with an arrow over them, such as [MATH: \overrightarrow{AB}.]

Content:
We will mostly stick to these notations. However, there are many possible notations for vectors. For example, sometimes a vector can be denoted as
[MATH: \vec{v}, \quad \overrightarrow{V}, \quad v, \quad \hat{v}.]
The rightmost notation, [MATH: \hat{v},] is usually used to represent unit vectors in particular.
